newsitem.title: GERMANY: German industry sees benefits in EMU.
newsitem.headline: German industry sees benefits in EMU.

text.p: German industry expects the labour market to protect the economy against external shocks after the introduction of a single European currency in 1999, business associations said on Monday.

"When exchange rates are fixed a buffer against real economic shocks is removed. The corrective function of exchange rates will have to be taken by greater flexibility, particularly in the labour market," said a joint statement by 16 organisations led by the Federation of German Industry (BDI).
To achieve this flexiblity, the business sector is counting on broad deregulation.
The single currency will protect German manufacturers against future appreciation of the mark against other currencies, which makes it harder for German companies to compete.
But many are unsure of its effects on the labour market and whether it will encourage workers to migrate from traditionally low-wage countries to countries with higher wages.
The German construction industry is trying to establish a minimum wage for all workers to protect itself against competition from low-wage countries.

The statement called on political leaders to establish a stability pact to ensure that participants in European Economic and Monetary Union (EMU) continue to maintain the strict convergence criteria even after the start of EMU.
The associations said they expect EMU to start with a small number of countries since budgetary convergence is behind schedule in most countries.
"The stability of the currency is paramount," the statement said, adding that the associations support Germany's efforts to meet the EMU criteria.

The rates at which national currencies will be exchanged for the new currency, to be called Euro, should be set as early as possible in 1998 after the list of initial participants is decided, they said.
